thesis: The manuscript argues that some artworks make an appreciator’s actual revision of a reasonably favored but false interpretation an aesthetically valuable activity. Settled foreknowledge can prevent that particular activity without preventing imaginative participation, excellent appreciation, or greater overall enjoyment. The loss can occur through voluntary or accidental disclosure, so it need not involve another person violating the appreciator’s wishes. Where delaying decisive information is inexpensive and both routes are attractive and feasible, this supplies a defeasible reason to preserve an initially uninformed encounter.
claimed_contribution: The strongest defensible contribution is a restricted explanation of one aesthetic opportunity: recognizing a work’s handling of interpretation through an interpretation one actually adopted and relinquished. Section 3 expressly disclaims originality for temporally enacted interpretation and for valuing interpretive activity. Sections 4–6 also reject the stronger claims that informed imagination is impossible, that uninformed appreciation is superior, or that preserving uncertainty always improves the total experience. The audit therefore tests the remaining combination of actual correction, expressive relevance, and loss without an overall setback, rather than attributing those rejected claims to the author.

findings.manuscript_location: §3, “Why this particular correction can matter”: “the reader recognizes the narrative’s handling of perspective in an interpretation she actually used and relinquished”; §4, “What informed imagination preserves”: “Reconstruction can preserve important parts of the experience.”
findings.claim: The literature discussion omits a directly relevant spoiler-specific predecessor: Daniele Molinari’s account of losing retrospective reinterpretation through advance knowledge.
findings.analysis: Molinari’s §3.2, pp. 88–89, argues that knowing the twist of The Sixth Sense prevents the viewer from retrospectively reassessing earlier scenes under a newly acquired interpretation. He distinguishes this pleasure from appreciating other cinematic features. This is substantive overlap with the manuscript’s unavailable interpretive route, beyond a shared interest in surprise. The omission is demonstrated; anticipation of the manuscript’s entire restricted thesis is not. See [Molinari’s article](https://www.argumenta.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/11/5-Argumenta-6-1-Daniele-Molinari-Spoiler-Alert.pdf).
findings.effect_on_conclusion: The removal of retrospective reinterpretation by spoilers cannot itself carry the novelty claim. The remaining contribution concerns a work making the appreciator’s own interpretive activity expressive subject matter, and the compatibility of losing that activity with a better informed encounter overall.
findings.repair_conditions: Compare the specific mechanism with Molinari’s argument and distinguish the manuscript’s evaluative premise and narrower scope. This requires clearer positioning, not abandonment of the central conclusion.

findings.manuscript_location: §6, “The modest priority of an uncompleted route”: “an uninformed encounter can normally be followed by informed reconsideration” and “This gives an initial encounter a kind of option-preserving priority.”
findings.claim: The sequencing rationale has an uncited antecedent in Richard Greene’s publicly recorded explanation of spoiler loss.
findings.analysis: A 2019 institutional record quotes Greene explaining that an unspoiled viewing leaves a later spoiled viewing available, whereas the initial opportunity cannot be recovered. The quoted phrase “the value of seeing it spoiled is still available” identifies the same directional argument. This establishes overlap with the recorded statement, not with every qualification in the inaccessible book. See [the institutional record](https://www.weber.edu/wsutoday/061219_spoileralert.html).
findings.effect_on_conclusion: The basic sequencing asymmetry is not a distinctive result here. The manuscript’s restrictions concerning time, adverse effects, feasibility, and informed choice remain substantive qualifications. No explicit false claim of priority appears in §6.
findings.repair_conditions: Acknowledge the antecedent and delimit the added qualifications. Consult the relevant book chapter before making a stronger claim about what Greene does or does not already allow.

surviving_contribution: The defensible remainder is an integration and restriction of existing ideas, not a new discovery that reading unfolds through revisions or that spoilers remove some first encounters. Its specific proposal is that actual, reasonable interpretive commitment and subsequent correction can constitute an apt response when the work makes that interpretive process part of its subject. Sections 3–5 distinguish this good from surprise, moral improvement, imaginative simulation, and merely receiving the correct answer. They also separate assistance that enables correction, an alternative discovery that bypasses correction, and disclosure that closes the opportunity. The opened sources do not establish that this complete argument has already been made. Conversely, this finite search cannot establish its priority. The two demonstrated omissions narrow the defensible novelty description without defeating the conditional aesthetic conclusion.
remaining_questions: Plausible objection, not a demonstrated defect: §3 grounds value in “this mode of responsive participation,” while §4 allows informed imagination to preserve much of the experience. The unresolved evaluative question is what makes actual correction aesthetically significant beyond its being a different activity. The manuscript identifies this disagreement and offers a work-specific answer; the cited precedents do not independently settle it.

Unanswered literature question: §3 says the argument “applies” Nguyen’s engagement account, and §5 distinguishes assistance from replacement. Nguyen also discusses guidance that sustains versus terminates engagement. How much of the application requires the additional condition that interpretation itself becomes the work’s expressive subject? See S4, manuscript pp. 14–17.

Access-dependent question: §1 attributes both an autonomy explanation and twist/puzzle exceptions to Levy. The abstract supports the former, but the relevant full sections could not be opened. Their exact scope, and the manuscript’s complete relationship to Levy’s qualifications, remain unverified.

Access-dependent novelty question: Greene’s complete discussion and Kivy’s chapters on first and repeated readings could further reduce the remainder. Neither book’s relevant full argument was accessible through the retrieved public pages.
limitations: This was a finite, predominantly English-language search across spoiler philosophy, reader-response theory, aesthetic engagement, and aesthetic discovery. It does not establish exhaustive originality or the absence of other close precedents.

The supplied Chasid and Nguyen archive links were blocked. Author-uploaded counterparts were opened elsewhere; their labels and relevant passages were checked, but the files were not established to be identical to the cited archive files.

The supplied Iser URL was inaccessible. An alternate scan supplied the relevant primary text and printed pagination. The JSTOR article page returned no usable record, so the issue metadata received less independent verification than the substantive attribution.

Greene’s book was available only through bibliographic and descriptive pages; its preview yielded no readable chapter text. The overlap finding is confined to directly attributed quotations in the institutional record. Fish’s Surprised by Sin was checked only through its opening two-page publisher preview, and Kivy’s book only through publisher metadata and section listings.

Source consultation was targeted to relevant passages, not a complete reading of every retrieved work. No empirical study was completed on voluntary forgetting or the frequency of the manuscript’s proposed experience. The opening scenario and the 0.6 example are hypothetical, not reported experimental results.

citation_audit.manuscript_location: §2, “A viewer implicated by the form”: “assigns surveillance a probability of 0.6” and “It does not show that 0.6 was too high when assigned.”
citation_audit.evidence: This is an illustrative stipulation, not an attributed formal result or empirical estimate. Learning that the less-favored possibility occurred does not by itself establish that the earlier probability was unreasonable. No external theorem or numerical evidence is claimed, so there is no missing formal-source attribution to repair.

citation_audit.manuscript_reference: Uncited practical claim concerning knowledge and replay.
citation_audit.manuscript_location: §4, “What informed imagination preserves”: “replay alone normally cannot undo recently acquired knowledge.”
citation_audit.evidence: The claim is explicitly qualified, and the manuscript allows forgetting and renewed uncertainty. It is consistent with the retrieved first-reading discussions, but this audit did not independently verify its psychological frequency or mechanisms. It should retain its practical qualification rather than be read as an experimentally established law.
